reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it presents a Telugu-language tutorial and discussion of work-from-home, referral, rewards, and account-opening programs, including demonstrations of a rewards interface and a OneCode dashboard, without clearly evidencing a deceptive scheme. The Current app is discussed in response to viewer questions with the speaker stating that it will not be recommended, and the subscription graphic is ordinary channel engagement rather than a financial offer.

opening.argument: The video repeatedly links monetary rewards to concrete actions rather than describing a harmless money-making topic. Viewers are directed to use “refer and earn,” share the option with family members, and expect 400–500 rupees from one person. Other offers connect payment to account activity: the speaker says a supposedly free demat account requires paying 25 rupees per month, while the displayed OneCode dashboard presents wallet payments after a purchase or account opening. This is a solicitation pathway in which registration, referral, or purchase is the condition for claiming an easy cash reward, fitting a low-barrier reward-acquisition scheme.

They are offering free demat account when you pay 25 per month

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling this a tutorial does not remove the solicitation. The defense's own examples show that viewers are told to share links so others can register or buy accounts, and the reward is expressly attached to that activity. The point is not merely that referral programs exist; it is that this video presents participation and another person's transaction as the route to payment, while the displayed flow also collects referral information.

citations.quote: if you share the website in whatsapp, then they can register and buy the account
they'll make entry only if you will give a compulsory referral code

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The cited material shows ordinary referral promotions, not a deceptive scheme. It does not establish that any reward was fabricated, that a payment failed, or that the account-opening terms were concealed. A referral code, registration fields, and a purchase-linked reward are consistent with promotional programs. The defense also correctly notes that the speaker refused to recommend the disputed Current app, which undercuts treating every offer discussed as an endorsement.

citations.quote: but I won't suggest you
After sharing their links with others they pay for it.

opening.argument: The risk signals are unusually concentrated: the video uses guaranteed-sounding payment language, specific payout timing, external referral routes, personal-data collection, and wallet withdrawals. One site is described as providing “100% percent payment” every month by the 21st, and the dashboard shows money flowing to a PayTM wallet after purchases or account completion. Registration is described as requiring a name, mobile number, and compulsory referral code. Taken together, these are not merely educational claims; they frame easy, predictable cash as the result of low-effort referrals and transactions, a classic warning pattern for a reward-acquisition solicitation.

citations.quote: this website has 100% percent payment within every month 21st
They can direct our bank account or direct money on it
give first and last name and mobile number to register

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense emphasizes the speaker's discussion of a supposedly fake app, but that does not answer the stronger signals in the promoted programs. A warning about one app can coexist with promotion of other offers that promise 100% payment, require personal details and referral codes, and route users toward account purchases. Nor does calling the on-screen graphic channel engagement explain the separate payout and registration material.

citations.quote: this website has 100% percent payment within every month 21st
they'll make entry only if you will give a compulsory referral code

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These are risk indicators, not proof of deception. “100% payment” is a claim about a promotional site's stated payout, but the record does not show that it was false or that users lost money. Names, phone numbers, referral codes, wallets, and withdrawal screens are normal mechanics for referral and rewards platforms. The evidence therefore supports ordinary promotion with conditions, not a demonstrated scam.

citations.quote: They will provide the opportunities.

opening.argument: The instructional framing functions as promotion because the speaker does not remain at the level of general advice. He names multiple services, supplies referral routes, explains how to enter a compulsory code, tells viewers to share links through WhatsApp, and describes the earnings available when other people register or buy. He even directs viewers to a site listing places where money can be earned by referral. That is an acquisition funnel: the tutorial format makes participation appear practical and trustworthy while channeling viewers toward recruitment-based commissions and transactions.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense calls this a discussion, but the operational instructions are promotional in effect: viewers are told where to find offers, how to use a referral code, and how to distribute the links so others can register or buy. The fact that the speaker also discusses doubts about Current does not neutralize the affirmative promotion of the other programs or the promised commission for bringing in participants.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The activity described is one-level referral promotion, not evidence of a recruitment matrix, downline, or tier qualification. The speaker explains that services pay when someone registers, purchases, or opens an account, which is compatible with ordinary affiliate marketing. The quoted instructions show how to participate but do not show coercion, concealment, fabricated rewards, or nonpayment. The format may be promotional without being a scam.
